The journey of the Venetian merchant Marco Polo, who left Venice in 1271 with his father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo and reached the court of Kublai Khan in about 1275. The older Polos had been to the khan once already and carried letters from the Pope.

They went overland through Persia and Central Asia, on routes kept open by the Mongol Empire. Marco says he served Kublai's Yuan government for seventeen years and travelled widely in China. The family came home by sea around 1295, escorting a Mongol princess to the Ilkhanate in Persia on the way.

Taken prisoner in a war with Genoa, Marco told his story to a fellow prisoner, the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa. Their book, known as The Travels of Marco Polo, described paper money, coal, the Grand Canal and cities far larger than any in Europe. Some readers doubted it then, and scholars still argue over parts of it. But it shaped Europe's picture of Asia for centuries, and Christopher Columbus owned a copy full of his notes.
